splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagreed on when actuarial assumptions used to calculate employer withdrawal liability under ERISA must be finalized. The split affected billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers in multiemployer pension plans. SCOTUS resolved the case.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability must be selected no later than the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers greater predictability.

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that a plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, allowing the use of more current data in calculating withdrawal liability.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. The split affected thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year. SCOTUS resolved the case.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled during the period a supervisee absconds, extending the court's authority to revoke supervised release beyond the original term.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory or common-law basis for tolling the term of supervised release when a supervisee absconds, and courts lack authority to extend punishment beyond the statutory term without explicit congressional authorization.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: Circuits split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face a categorical bar under § 2244(b)(1) from raising any claim they previously presented in a successive § 2255 motion, in addition to the separate requirements in § 2255(h). The outcome determines whether federal prisoners face stricter gatekeeping than Congress intended. SCOTUS resolved the case.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the categorical bar in § 2244(b)(1) against relitigating previously presented claims applies to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions, imposing an additional gatekeeping requirement.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, meaning they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagreed on whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures. The split raised concerns about whether election disputes must be funneled into post-election litigation if standing is denied pre-election. SCOTUS resolved the case.

positions.label: Candidate has standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge state election laws before Election Day based on competitive injury from allegedly unlawful ballot-counting rules.

positions.label: Candidate lacks standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate for federal office does not have Article III standing to challenge mail-in ballot counting rules pre-election absent a concrete, particularized injury.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes precedence over deference to agency interpretations (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous provisions in the Sentencing Guidelines that increase criminal penalties.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether courts should apply lenity or defer to the Sentencing Commission's commentary when Guidelines provisions are ambiguous in criminal sentencing contexts. At least three circuits hold lenity trumps deference, while the Third Circuit held deference trumps lenity. The split has deepened after Loper Bright overruled Chevron.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes precedence over agency deference when interpreting ambiguous criminal provisions, including Sentencing Guidelines, preventing agencies from expanding criminal liability through interpretive guidance.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency deference to the Sentencing Commission's commentary controls over the rule of lenity when interpreting ambiguous Sentencing Guidelines provisions, even in criminal contexts.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any one criterion disqualifies).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether 'and' in § 3553(f)(1) means a defendant must meet all three criminal-history criteria to be disqualified from safety-valve relief, or whether meeting any single criterion is disqualifying. The split leads to dramatically different sentences for defendants with identical criminal histories depending on the circuit.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required to disqualify
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' in its ordinary conjunctive sense.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) disqualifies a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as distributive or disjunctive in context.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' in U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses like conspiracy, such that Application Note 1 (which includes conspiracy) exceeds the Commission's interpretive authority under Kisor v. Wilkie.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether conspiracy and other inchoate offenses qualify as 'controlled substance offenses' under the career-offender guideline. Some circuits defer to Application Note 1's inclusion of inchoate offenses, while others hold the guideline text is unambiguous and does not include them. The Sentencing Commission has since amended the text, but the split affects cases sentenced under earlier guidelines.

positions.label: Application Note 1 is valid — inchoate offenses qualify
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1's inclusion of conspiracy and other inchoate offenses in the definition of 'controlled substance offense' is a permissible interpretation entitled to deference under Stinson/Kisor.

positions.label: Guideline text is unambiguous — inchoate offenses excluded
positions.summary: Holds that the text of § 4B1.2(b) unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses and that Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the guideline beyond its plain meaning, failing Kisor's threshold requirement of genuine ambiguity.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state-scheduled substance is not controlled under federal law (the Controlled Substances Act).
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the substance at issue to be federally scheduled or whether any state-controlled substance suffices. The split affects career-offender and other sentencing enhancements for defendants with prior state drug convictions.

positions.label: State scheduling suffices — no federal-law limitation
positions.summary: Holds that a 'controlled substance offense' under the Guidelines includes offenses under state law even if the substance is not federally scheduled, because the text refers broadly to 'an offense under state law' without a federal-law limitation.

positions.label: Federal scheduling required
positions.summary: Holds that a prior state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' only if the substance is also controlled under federal law, applying a categorical approach that requires overlap with federal schedules.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether non-retroactive changes in sentencing law (such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)) may be considered as an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether district courts may consider non-retroactive changes in law — alone or in combination with other factors — as extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release. The Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment to U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6) attempted to permit such consideration, but some circuits hold the Commission exceeded its authority. SCOTUS has granted cert on a related question.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may be considered
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law may contribute to or constitute 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' for compassionate release, either alone or in combination with other factors, consistent with the Sentencing Commission's 2024 policy statement.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot be considered
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in sentencing law cannot serve as an extraordinary and compelling reason for compassionate release, whether alone or in combination with other factors, because allowing such consideration would circumvent Congress's decision not to make the change retroactive.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly impose revocation sentences to punish defendants for violations of supervised release, or whether revocation sentences must serve only the purposes of supervised release itself.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Sentencing Reform Act permits district courts to impose revocation sentences that are explicitly punitive in nature. The Sixth Circuit allows district courts to punish defendants at revocation, placing it at an extreme of a circuit split, while other circuits hold revocation sentences may not be imposed for punitive purposes.

positions.label: Punishment is permissible at revocation
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release when imposing revocation sentences under 18 U.S.C. § 3583(e).

positions.label: Punishment is not a proper purpose at revocation
positions.summary: Holds that revocation sentences must serve the purposes of supervised release and may not be imposed to punish the defendant for the violation itself, consistent with the statute's focus on deterrence and protection of the public.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the appeal deadline for an order denying a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees in a criminal case is governed by the civil deadline (60 days) or the criminal deadline (14 days).
splits.description: Circuits split on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to a criminal case (subject to the 60-day civil appeal deadline) or a criminal matter (subject to the 14-day criminal appeal deadline). The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 60-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) applies.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: United States v. Manchester Farming Partnership

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion remains part of the criminal case, so the 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b) applies.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners challenging conditions of confinement or BOP decisions regarding terms of imprisonment (such as First Step Act time credits) must proceed under habeas corpus (28 U.S.C. § 2241) or may alternatively use civil rights actions (e.g., Bivens).
splits.description: Circuits have long disagreed on whether challenges to conditions or terms of confinement that do not directly challenge the fact or duration of imprisonment must be brought as habeas petitions or may also proceed as civil rights claims. This affects federal prisoners challenging BOP decisions on First Step Act earned time credits and prerelease custody.

positions.label: Habeas is the exclusive remedy for duration-related claims
positions.summary: Holds that when a prisoner's claim effectively challenges the duration of confinement (including eligibility for prerelease custody), habeas corpus under § 2241 is the exclusive federal remedy.

positions.label: Conditions claims may proceed outside habeas
positions.summary: Holds that prisoners may bring civil rights or non-habeas claims to challenge conditions of confinement or BOP administrative decisions, even when those decisions affect the timing of release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in property equity belong to the bankruptcy estate or to debtors who convert in good faith from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether post-petition appreciation in property value inures to the bankruptcy estate upon a good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7. The Ninth Circuit held that appreciation belongs to the estate, while other courts have held it belongs to the debtor. The split affects whether debtors lose the benefit of property appreciation when they convert.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that post-petition, pre-conversion increases in equity are property of the estate upon conversion under § 348(f)(1)(A), based on the broad definition of 'property of the estate' in § 541(a).

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that under § 348(f)(1)(A), only the property as valued at the time of the original petition filing enters the converted estate, meaning post-petition appreciation belongs to the debtor in a good-faith conversion.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether RLUIPA permits suits for money damages against state prison officials in their individual capacities. The question implicates Spending Clause limits on Congress's power to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds. SCOTUS has taken up the issue.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text clearly authorizes suits for money damages against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Landor v. Louisiana Dep't of Corrections

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, or that Congress lacks Spending Clause power to impose such personal liability.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may encompass claims that could also be raised in habeas proceedings under § 2255, such as claims of legal error in the original conviction or sentence. Some circuits permit courts to consider such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) may not be used as a substitute for § 2255.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider claims related to potential errors in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor among others in the extraordinary-and-compelling-reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: May not use § 3582 as substitute for § 2255
positions.summary: Holds that compassionate release under § 3582(c)(1)(A) may not serve as a vehicle for claims that properly belong under § 2255, and that alleged legal errors in the underlying conviction or sentence are not cognizable as extraordinary and compelling reasons.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments under federal civil rights law?
splits.description: The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve disagreement among circuits over the standards for discrimination claims against hospitality and business operators, including questions about liability and available remedies. The Second Circuit's approach was deemed sufficiently unsettled to warrant review.

positions.label: Broader liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that broader standards apply to discrimination claims against business establishments, potentially allowing for more expansive remedies.

positions.label: Narrower liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that narrower standards govern such claims, limiting the scope of liability and available remedies for discrimination in public accommodations.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
